precepts.text: Into the second tabernacle went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and the errors of the people, the Holy Ghost signifying that the way into the holiest was not yet made manifest, standing only in meats and drinks and divers washings, carnal ordinances imposed until the time of reformation, which is the coming of Christ.
precepts.point: Hiram makes the lavers, shovels, and basins, and finishes all the work he made for Solomon for the house of the Lord: the two pillars, the two bowls of the chapters, the two networks, four hundred pomegranates, the ten bases and their lavers, the one sea, and the twelve oxen under it. All these vessels are of bright brass, cast in the plain of Jordan in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan, left unweighed because they were exceeding many.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

precepts.why:
“But into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood, which he offered for himself, and for the errors of the people: The Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest, while as the first tabernacle was yet standing”.

It was “a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience; Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.” The time of reformation is the coming of Christ.

That is what all Hiram’s bright brass served: the lavers, the shovels, the basons, the ten bases and ten lavers, the one sea on twelve oxen. They were for the washings and the sacrifices of that service, vessels so many “Solomon left all the vessels unweighed”, all belonging to the carnal ordinances that stood until Christ came.

precepts.text: The workman was a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali, his father a man of Tyre, filled with wisdom to work in brass.
precepts.point: Huram promised to cut wood out of Lebanon as much as Solomon needed and bring it in floats by sea to Joppa, from where it would be carried up to Jerusalem. These floats are like the large cargo ships and barges seen today upon the rivers and the seas.

note.label: 2 Chronicles 2: Solomon Prepares to Build the House

precepts.why:
“He was a widow’s son of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass: and he was filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass.”

Chronicles says the same workman was “The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre.” There is no contradiction. His mother was of the tribe of Naphtali, but she was of the city of Dan, which lay within the land of Naphtali. This is cleared up by using the Bible dictionary and the maps, and by chasing the references.

He was “skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving.”

points: Solomon is thirteen years building his own house and finishes all his houses, including the house of the forest of Lebanon, a hundred cubits long, fifty broad, and thirty high, upon four rows of cedar pillars with cedar beams, with windows in three rows, light against light. He makes a porch of pillars, and a porch for the throne, the porch of judgment, covered with cedar from floor to floor.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: Solomon's throne sat back off a porch of judgment, an area before which men would stand while the throne rose behind and above them under its own covering. He also makes a house for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken to wife, a marriage made, as marriages were in that time, for political gain and standing among the nations.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: All these buildings are of costly hewn stones, sawed with saws within and without, from the foundation to the coping, great stones of ten and eight cubits. The great court round about is set with three rows of hewn stone and a row of cedar beams, matching the inner court of the house of the Lord and its porch.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: King Solomon sends and fetches Hiram out of Tyre, a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali, whose father was a man of Tyre and a worker in brass. He was filled with wisdom, understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass.

Here the mother is named of the tribe of Naphtali, while in Chronicles she is called of the daughters of Dan, meaning she lived in the area of Dan but was of the tribe of Naphtali. The craftsman was of Israel's lineage, sent to do the brass work of the temple.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: Hiram casts two pillars of brass, each eighteen cubits high, and two chapters of molten brass of five cubits each to set upon their tops, with nets of checker work and wreaths of chain work, seven for each chapter. The chapters are the ornamented capital at the top of each pillar, the crowning molding.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: The pillars are wrought with pomegranates in two rows and lily work, and Solomon sets them up in the porch of the temple, calling the right one Jachin, which means established, and the left one Boaz, which means strength. So the work of the pillars is finished.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: Hiram makes a molten sea, ten cubits from brim to brim, round, five cubits high, with a line of thirty cubits compassing it, and knops beneath the brim in two rows cast when it was cast. This great brazen basin held water for the washings.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: Hiram makes ten bases of brass, four cubits long and broad and three high, with borders of lions, oxen, and cherubims, set upon four brazen wheels like chariot wheels with axletrees, naves, fellows, and spokes all molten. Upon each base he sets a laver of brass containing forty baths, five bases on the right side of the house and five on the left, with the molten sea set on the right side eastward toward the south.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: Hiram makes the lavers, shovels, and basins, and finishes all the work he made for Solomon for the house of the Lord: the two pillars, the two bowls of the chapters, the two networks, four hundred pomegranates, the ten bases and their lavers, the one sea, and the twelve oxen under it. All these vessels are of bright brass, cast in the plain of Jordan in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan, left unweighed because they were exceeding many.

note.label: 1 Kings 7: Solomon's House and the Brass Work of the Temple

points: Solomon makes all the vessels of the house of the Lord: the altar of gold, the table of gold for the showbread, the candlesticks of pure gold, five on each side, with the flowers, lamps, tongs, bowls, snuffers, basins, spoons, and censers of pure gold, and the hinges of gold for the doors. When the work is ended, Solomon brings in the things David his father had dedicated, the silver, gold, and vessels, and puts them among the treasures of the house of the Lord.
